Ideas about sleep
Spot the thoughts that add pressure, and soften them.

Some ideas about sleep are very common. They seem reasonable, but they increase tension at bedtime, and so wakefulness. For each one, ask yourself whether it crosses your mind, then read the more accurate version.

string-array.name: cog_beliefs_steps
string-array.item: “I need 8 hours of sleep to feel good.”\n\nThe need for sleep varies from one person to another, and from one night to the next. Many adults do well with less than 8 hours.
“If I sleep badly tonight, tomorrow is ruined.”\n\nAfter a bad night, people often function better than they fear. The tiredness is real, but rarely as strong as expected.
“I have to catch up on sleep by staying in bed longer.”\n\nStaying in bed longer makes sleep lighter and more broken. A steady schedule is what consolidates it.
“I have no control over my sleep anymore.”\n\nYou act on everything that helps it: your schedule, a bed kept for sleep, the pace of your evenings. Sleep then comes on its own.

“Insomnia is going to damage my health.”\n\nIt is an understandable worry, but thinking about it at night keeps you awake. Insomnia can be treated, and the method you are following is the one recommended first.

resources.string: Putting your day to rest
Set your worries down early in the evening, so you don\'t take them to bed.
When you lie down, the mind often uses the quiet to replay the day and plan the next one. This routine gives it another, earlier moment to do so.

string-array.name: cog_winddown_steps
string-array.item: Early in the evening, at least an hour before bed, take fifteen quiet minutes with a sheet of paper and a pen.
Write down what is on your mind: work, family, things to do. Without trying to solve everything.
Next to each worry, write the next small step, or “nothing to do tonight”.
Put the sheet away. If a worry comes back in bed, remind yourself that it is written down and that you will deal with it tomorrow.

resources.string: Stop chasing sleep
Trying hard to sleep keeps sleep away. Try the opposite.
Sleep cannot be ordered: the harder you try to fall asleep, the more awake you stay. This exercise takes that pressure away.

string-array.name: cog_paradox_steps
string-array.item: In bed, with the light off, keep your eyes open in the dark and calmly tell yourself that you will keep them open a little longer.
Do nothing to fall asleep. Don\'t look at the time. Simply let the time pass.
If after a long while you feel tense, follow the usual rule: get up, and go back to bed when sleep comes.

resources.string: Back to the most likely
Four questions for when a bad night worries you.

When the night is going badly, the mind often imagines the worst for the next day. These questions help bring you back to what is most likely. You can answer them in your head or on paper, in the evening.

string-array.name: cog_decatastrophize_steps
string-array.item: What exactly am I afraid of for tomorrow?
What actually happened the other times, after a bad night?
What is most likely this time?
If tomorrow is hard, what would help me get through it? A break, a walk, a simpler task…

resources.string: Relaxing the body
Progressive muscle relaxation, in ten minutes.

Do this in the evening, sitting or lying down, preferably out of bed the first few times. For each part of the body: tense gently for five seconds, then relax for fifteen seconds, noticing the difference. Stop if tensing a muscle hurts.

string-array.name: cog_relax_steps
string-array.item: Hands and forearms: clench your fists, then let go.
Arms: bend your elbows and tighten your biceps, then let go.
Shoulders and neck: raise your shoulders towards your ears, then let them drop.
Face: wrinkle your forehead and squeeze your eyes shut, then relax your whole face.
Stomach and back: pull in your stomach and straighten your back, then let go while breathing slowly.
Legs and feet: stretch your legs and point your toes, then let go. Stay in this relaxed state for a few moments.
